kernel.def: The core of the operating system. It runs every program, hands out memory and CPU time, and talks to the hardware. All containers on a machine share its kernel.

operating-system.def: The software that runs a computer, like Ubuntu, Windows or macOS: the kernel plus the basic tools and libraries around it.

virtual-machine.def: A whole pretend computer running inside a real one, with its own operating system and kernel.

hypervisor.def: The software that creates and runs virtual machines, sharing the real hardware between them.

container.def: A normal program running on your machine, walled off so it gets its own files, network and process list. It's started from an image.

image.def: A read-only package holding an app and everything it needs to run: files, libraries and settings. Containers are started from images.

layer.def: One slice of an image: the files a single Dockerfile step added or changed. An image is a stack of layers.

registry.def: A server that stores images so you can upload (push) and download (pull) them, like Docker Hub or GitHub's GHCR.

tag.def: A readable name for one version of an image, like 1.2.0 or latest. Tags can be moved to point at a different image later.

digest.def: A fingerprint (SHA-256 hash) of an image's exact contents. Unlike a tag, it can never point at anything else.

dockerfile.def: A text file with step-by-step instructions for building an image.

daemon.def: A program that runs in the background. The Docker daemon (dockerd) does the real work; the docker command only sends it requests.

cli.def: Command-line interface: a program you use by typing commands in a terminal, like docker.

namespace.def: A Linux feature that gives a process its own private view of something: its own process list, network, hostname or files.

cgroup.def: Control group: a Linux feature that limits and measures how much CPU, memory and other resources a group of processes can use.

process.def: A running program. The operating system gives each one an ID number (its PID) and its own memory.

pid-1.def: The first process in a container, which is your app. It has a special job: it must handle shutdown signals itself, or they're ignored.

signal.def: A short message the operating system sends to a process, like 'please stop' (SIGTERM) or 'stop now' (SIGKILL).

sigterm.def: The polite 'please shut down' signal. A program can catch it, finish its work and exit cleanly. docker stop sends it first.

sigkill.def: The 'stop right now' signal. It can't be caught or ignored: the process just ends, mid-task if need be.

exit-code.def: A number a program returns when it ends. 0 means success; anything else means something went wrong.

oom-killer.def: Out-of-memory killer: the part of the kernel that ends a process when memory runs out or a memory limit is reached.

userland.def: Everything in an operating system except the kernel: the shell, tools, libraries and config files. An image carries a userland, never a kernel.

c-library.def: The low-level library nearly every program uses to talk to the kernel. Debian and Ubuntu use glibc; Alpine uses the smaller musl, which some software isn't built for.

build-context.def: The folder docker build sends to the builder. COPY can only see files inside it.

buildkit.def: Docker's build engine. It runs your Dockerfile's steps, caches their results, and runs independent steps in parallel.

build-cache.def: Saved results of earlier build steps. If a step's inputs haven't changed, Docker reuses the saved result instead of running it again.

port.def: A numbered door on a machine where network traffic arrives. A web server might listen on port 80 or 3000.

localhost.def: A special address that always means 'this same machine'. Inside a container, it means that container, not your computer.

ip-address.def: The numeric address of a machine or container on a network, like 172.17.0.2.

dns.def: The network's phone book: it turns names like db or example.com into IP addresses.

bridge.def: A virtual network switch inside the host that containers plug into, so they can talk to each other and reach the outside.

nat.def: Network address translation: rewriting addresses on network traffic, so containers can share the host's address to reach the internet, and so a host port can lead to a container.

env-var.def: A named setting, like PORT=3000, that a program reads when it starts. It's how containers receive their configuration.

volume.def: Storage that Docker manages outside any container, so data survives when containers are deleted and replaced.

bind-mount.def: A folder from your own machine shown inside a container. It's not a copy: both sides see the same files.

tmpfs.def: A folder that lives only in memory. It's fast, never touches the disk, and is wiped when the container stops.

healthcheck.def: A command Docker runs regularly inside a container to check the app actually works, not just that it's running.

restart-policy.def: A rule telling Docker whether to start a container again when its process stops, and in which cases.

compose.def: A tool that starts a whole multi-container app, with its networks and volumes, from one YAML file.

yaml.def: A simple text format for settings that uses indentation to show structure. Compose files are written in it.

reverse-proxy.def: A server that sits in front of your app, receives every request first, and forwards it on. Nginx is a popular one.

nginx.def: A fast, widely used web server, often placed in front of apps as a reverse proxy.

postgres.def: A popular open-source SQL database, often called Postgres.

redis.def: A very fast in-memory data store, often used as a cache.

cache.def: A quick-to-reach copy of data that's slow to fetch, kept so the next request can skip the slow trip.

cve.def: A public ID for a known security bug, like CVE-2024-1234. Scanners match the packages in an image against lists of CVEs.

scanner.def: A tool that lists every package in an image and checks each one against databases of known security bugs.

capability.def: One specific slice of root's power in Linux, like changing file owners. Containers can be given or denied each one separately.

root.def: The all-powerful administrator account on Linux, with user ID 0.

uid.def: User ID: the number Linux uses to identify a user. Root is 0; names like node are just labels for numbers.

secret.def: Anything that grants access: a password, an API token, a private key.

ci.def: Continuous integration: a server automatically builds and checks your code every time it changes, for example with GitHub Actions.

github-actions.def: GitHub's built-in CI service. It runs the steps you describe in a YAML workflow file whenever your code changes.

architecture.def: The instruction set a CPU understands. amd64 is most Intel and AMD machines; arm64 is Apple Silicon Macs and many newer servers. Programs are built for one of them.

emulation.def: Running a program built for one CPU type on another by translating its instructions on the fly. It works, but slowly.

vps.def: Virtual private server: a small virtual machine you rent from a cloud provider and control completely.

ssh.def: A secure way to log in to another machine and run commands on it over the network.

firewall.def: Rules that decide which network traffic may enter or leave a machine.

tls.def: Encryption for web traffic. HTTPS is HTTP sent over TLS: the padlock in your browser's address bar.

lockfile.def: A file that records the exact version of every dependency, so every install gets the same ones. For npm it's package-lock.json.

dependency.def: A package of someone else's code that your app uses, like Express or pg.

hash.def: A fingerprint calculated from content. Change a single byte and the hash comes out completely different.

oci.def: Open Container Initiative: the shared standard for image and container formats, so images work with Docker, Podman and Kubernetes alike.

kubernetes.def: A system that runs containers across many machines, restarting and moving them automatically as needed.

orchestrator.def: A system that runs and manages containers across many machines for you. Kubernetes is the best known.

seccomp.def: A Linux feature that blocks a program from making certain risky requests to the kernel.

copy-on-write.def: A trick where a file is shared until someone changes it; only then is a private copy made for them.

stdout.def: A program's two standard output streams: normal output (stdout) and errors (stderr). Docker records both as the container's logs.

api.def: A program other programs talk to over the network. The notes API answers HTTP requests with JSON.

typescript.def: JavaScript with type annotations. It's compiled (or has its types stripped) into plain JavaScript before Node runs it.

image-index.def: A list that points to one image per CPU type under a single tag, so each machine pulls the one it can run.

attestation.def: Extra metadata attached to an image describing how and from what it was built.

ghcr.def: GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io): GitHub's registry for container images.

docker-hub.def: Docker's public registry, home of official images like nginx, node and postgres.

alpine.def: A very small Linux distribution, popular as a base image because it's only a few megabytes.

debian.def: A long-standing Linux distribution. Most official images, including node and postgres, are built on it.

distroless.def: Images containing only your app's runtime and its libraries: no shell and no package manager.

multi-stage.def: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages: you build in one and copy only the results into a small final one.

trivy.def: A free, open-source vulnerability scanner for images.
